Well, no, I wouldn't say I've gotten lost. I know my way around town just fine. I've lived in this same house for forty-two years, after all. We bought it back in 1981, right after the big blizzard. Oh, that blizzard was something else! The snow was piled so high against the front door we couldn't even open it. My husband had to climb out the window in the guest room just to shovel a path so we could get to the grocery store. 

And speaking of the grocery store, they've completely rearranged the aisles at the Piggly Wiggly down the street. It's maddening! I went in there last Tuesday just for some milk and a loaf of bread, and I ended up wandering around for twenty minutes because they moved the dairy section all the way to the back left corner. Why do they do that? Just when you get used to where everything is, they go and switch it all up. The young man working there—he couldn't have been more than sixteen, still had braces—he tried to tell me it was to "improve the shopping experience." I told him the only thing it improved was my step count for the day! 

But no, I know who my family is, certainly. My daughter came over just yesterday. She brought me a pot of those lovely yellow chrysanthemums. Though I really prefer the purple ones... but I didn't tell her that, of course. No need to look a gift horse in the mouth, as they say. But I knew it was her, and I know my way around, unless the grocery store goes and changes things on me again.

I told her to buy that special pet-safe salt for her walkway because of her little terrier, but did she listen? No. \n\nAnyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the fogginess. I just can't seem to keep things straight. I'll be sitting by the phone with my list, and I completely lose track of which volunteer I already called to cover the afternoon shifts. It's just very frustrating to feel this mixed up.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me roughly when you first started noticing this mental fogginess and memory trouble—was it weeks, months, or longer ago?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think... it must have been about four months ago. Yes, right around the time we had that awful water damage. A pipe just burst out of nowhere in the guest bathroom! It completely ruined the floor and pushed us right into a full remodel. We had to tear up all the old linoleum, which, honestly, I wasn't too sad about because it was this dreadful pea-green color from the seventies. I always thought it looked exactly like canned split pea soup. \n\nSo now we're doing the remodel and I've been looking at new tiles. Usually, I'm out there every morning checking for those awful hornworms—they can strip a plant bare in a day, you know. Disgusting things. It's just... there, I suppose.\n\nDoctor: When you notice these memory slips, like misplacing your glasses or losing track of calls, how much does it worry or upset you—would you say you're quite distressed by it, or does it not bother you all that much?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose it bothers me a little bit, but not terribly. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, my husband has certainly noticed something. He says I move like I'm wading through mud lately. Even just getting up from my chair to answer the phone or sort through the mail... it just takes me such a long time now. And speaking of the mail, the postman we have now, he's just terrible about putting our letters in the right box. 

Just last Thursday, I got a whole stack of mail meant for the Henderson's down the street. They live in that big yellow house on the corner, the one with the wrap-around porch. Mrs. Henderson planted the most beautiful hydrangeas along the front walkway this year. Huge, blue blooms. She told me the trick is to put coffee grounds in the soil to make them that vibrant blue color. I tried that once with my roses, but it didn't seem to do much. My husband always said my roses were beautiful anyway, though. We used to have a whole row of them along the back fence before we put the patio in. 

But yes, my movements are definitely slower, like I'm wading through mud, just to get up and get that misdelivered mail.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, no, I wouldn't say I feel guilty or worthless... I mean, I don't think so. Hopeless? Not really. I try to keep a positive outlook, you know? My mother always used to say, "Count your blessings, not your troubles." She was a very wise woman, my mother. She grew up during the Depression, so she knew a thing or two about hard times. She used to tell us stories about how they would make soup out of potato peels and whatever vegetables they could scrounge up from the garden. 

They lived on a little farm out in Ohio. I visited there once when I was a little girl. I remember they had this big red barn, and my uncle let me ride on the tractor. It was a John Deere, bright green. My grandson Tommy loves tractors. When he was a toddler, he had this little toy one that he would push all over the living room floor, making engine noises. "Vroom, vroom," he'd go, right over the rug. 

That rug was a Persian replica I found at an estate sale. It had these intricate patterns, mostly deep reds and navy blues. Estate sales can be such a treasure trove if you get there early enough. You have to be there right when they open the doors, otherwise all the good stuff is gone. I once found a beautiful set of silver spoons... but anyway, no, I don't feel unusually guilty or hopeless. I just try to take things one day at a time.

They show every single fingerprint! \n\nBut... oh, yes, the fogginess. It's been about four months. Right since that pipe burst.\n\nDoctor: Over these past four months, have you been feeling noticeably sad, down, or less interested in things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, actually. I just... I don't seem to care about much of anything anymore. It's the strangest feeling. Things I used to just love, they just sit there now. Like my watercolors. The male is just brilliant red, especially against the snow in the winter. Though we haven't had much snow this year, have we? It's been so unseasonably warm. \n\nMy tomato plants are the same way. Usually, I'm out there every morning checking for those awful hornworms—they can strip a plant bare in a day, you know. Disgusting things. I just haven't had the heart for it. And I love line dancing. We were learning the Electric Slide, which sounds so outdated, I know, but it's marvelous exercise for the joints. But lately... I just don't want to do any of it.\n\nDoctor: Over these past four months, have you noticed any changes in your sleep, such as trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up much earlier than usual?\n\nPatient: Well, my sleep... I suppose I haven't really noticed any big changes there. I've always been a bit of a light sleeper anyway, ever since my husband passed. He used to snore terribly, you know. Sounded like a freight train rolling through the bedroom! I used to have to wear those little foam earplugs, the bright orange ones. Well... yes, I suppose things have gotten a bit muddled lately. I've actually missed a couple of doctor visits, which isn't like me at all, and I completely tangled up the schedule for the senior center. Oh, the senior center is usually such a nice time. I used to be so good at that, you know. I kept a little metal Rolodex with all the handymen's numbers, very sturdy little thing, right by the kitchen phone. It's just... there, I suppose.\n\nDoctor: When you notice these memory slips, like misplacing your glasses or losing track of calls, how much does it worry or upset you—would you say you're quite distressed by it, or does it not bother you all that much?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose it bothers me a little bit, but not terribly. She has this giant keychain with a big fluffy pink ball on it—looks like a rabbit's foot, but she says it's faux fur. She bought it at a craft fair over at the Methodist church last November. \n\nThey always have the best craft fairs there. They sell these homemade jams, the strawberry-rhubarb is just to die for. Last time I went to a potluck, I brought my famous green bean casserole. Everyone always asks for the recipe, but I never give them the secret ingredient. It's a tiny dash of nutmeg, if you can believe it! My grandmother taught me that. It's just part of life, I figure.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any physical changes recently, such as a tremor or shaking in your hands, stiffness in your muscles, or your movements or walking becoming slower than before?\n\nPatient: Well, my husband has certainly noticed something. Well... when they remind me, I just... I don't know, it just doesn't ring a bell. Even when my husband explains it, it's like he's talking about something that happened to someone else. It's so frustrating, you know? It makes me feel like I'm losing my mind.

It's just... there, I suppose.\n\nDoctor: When you notice these memory slips, like misplacing your glasses or losing track of calls, how much does it worry or upset you—would you say you're quite distressed by it, or does it not bother you all that much?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose it bothers me a little bit, but not terribly. I mean, we all forget things as we get older, don't we? Like my friend Martha, she's constantly losing her keys. Well, I'm not really sure about that. I haven't noticed anything like that, to be honest. 

But speaking of noticing things, I was looking out my kitchen window just yesterday at the bird feeder. My husband put it up for me—it's a lovely little cedar one, shaped like a miniature barn with a little green roof. But those squirrels, oh my goodness, they are just relentless! They climb right up the metal pole, no matter how much grease he puts on it. He actually tried using Crisco last week. Crisco! Can you imagine? 

My mother used to bake the most wonderful cherry pie crusts with Crisco. She always said the absolute secret to a truly flaky crust was keeping the shortening ice cold. Finally found them sitting right on top of the microwave. Now why on earth would I put them there? I was just trying to heat up a cup of water for my peppermint tea. My mother always swore by peppermint tea for digestion, you know. I always buy three jars, one for me, one for my daughter, and one just in case I need a quick host gift. You never know when you're going to be invited over for a potluck or something. Last time I went to a potluck, I brought my famous green bean casserole. Everyone always asks for the recipe, but I never give them the secret ingredient. It's a tiny dash of nutmeg, if you can believe it! My grandmother taught me that. She was a wonderful cook, could make a feast out of a ham bone and a few potatoes. \n\nSo, no, I wouldn't say I'm overly distressed about the memory slips. It's just part of life, I figure.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any physical changes recently, such as a tremor or shaking in your hands, stiffness in your muscles, or your movements or walking becoming slower than before?\n\nPatient: Well, my husband has certainly noticed something. Medical conditions? Oh, no, nothing like that. My doctor says I'm healthy as a horse for my age. 

My father used to say that, actually—"healthy as a horse." He grew up on a farm in Ohio, you see. They had draft horses, the big ones with the feathery hair around their hooves. Clydesdales, I think they're called. Or maybe Percherons? Well, anyway, they were massive animals. Antique shops are so fascinating, don't you think? You just never know what you're going to find. I was in one just last month looking for a replacement saucer for my teacup set—it's a Royal Doulton, the Old Country Roses pattern. Such a classic design with the gold banding. I was heartbroken when I chipped the saucer washing it. I always wash my good china by hand, never in the dishwasher. Dishwashers are so harsh on the glaze. My daughter just throws everything in hers, even her good knives. I keep telling her it dulls the blades, but she says she doesn't have the time to stand at the sink. 

Everyone is just in such a rush these days, always hurrying from one thing to the next. Nobody stops to just enjoy a quiet afternoon anymore...
